stories.title: The Eviction Candidate
stories.text: After Blackstone, the world’s largest corporate landlord and private real estate owner, made news for ramping up evictions and raising rents in 2023, Michigan Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers invested as much as $250,000 in Blackstone’s private real estate trust — investments he still holds today. Now, on the campaign trail, the former state representative has proposed an affordable housing strategy described as a “ gimme to homebuilders ” that would create zones where residential developers would pay no federal taxes. After Blackstone purchased five university housing apartments in Rogers’ home state in 2022, the company raised students' rent by 26 percent over the following three years — double the area’s average rent increase. In early 2023, Blackstone started eviction proceedings against hundreds of tenants throughout the U.S. while sunsetting its pandemic-era rent forbearance programs. stories.title: The falsehoods billionaires are mailing to Ohio voters
stories.text: V-PAC is a super PAC supporting Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign for governor in Ohio. Most of its $42 million war chest has come from a handful of billionaires, including Jeff Yass ($20 million), Ross Stevens ($6 million), Elon Musk ($5 million), Ratmir Timashev ($5 million), and Bill Ackman ($1 million). Popular Information obtained a V-PAC mailer attacking Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton from an Ohio voter through Paid For By , our new web app. Paid For By instantly gives voters detailed information about the groups sending political mailers. Popular Information then reviews everything submitted. The anti-Acton mailer is a vivid illustration of why more journalistic scrutiny of political mail is necessary. Every claim on V-PAC’s mailer is either flatly false or deeply misleading. The lead claim of the flyer, which inexplicably includes the symbol of the communist party, is that Acton “was called ‘incompetent’ to the Ohio State Medical Board.” This is not true. To support its claim, V-PAC cites Acton’s 1994 “Application for Certificate – Medicine or Osteopathic Medicine” with the State Medical Board of Ohio. stories.title: Why Bagram Air Base Remains a Target Five Years After U.S. Exited Afghanistan
stories.text: This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. BAGRAM, Afghanistan— “They are back,” said Abdul Maroof, a 38-year-old resident of Kabul. “God knows what they are doing, but they are back and the Taliban are hiding it.” Maroof had not been to Bagram himself. Like many in the capital, he heard the story from friends, relatives, and social media feeds insisting that foreign military vehicles and low-flying aircraft had been spotted near the perimeter. In Kabul, where political anxiety fuels a relentless rumor mill, the claim is repeated as settled fact. For months, viral videos and online commentary have alleged that U.S. forces quietly reclaimed the sprawling airfield north of the capital—or that the Taliban now manage it under a secret pact with Washington. stories.title: Your Tap Water Could Have A 67 Percent Markup
stories.text: Data from the 500 largest neighborhood water systems in the U.S. reveals that, in the last decade, the cost of household drinking water increased faster than inflation, grocery prices, and median income — thanks, in part, to for-profit water systems. A brand-new report by the climate group Food & Water Watch finds that household drinking water costs in the communities studied increased by an average of 62 percent between 2015 and 2025. Households that rely on for-profit businesses for their water supply are significantly worse off: In 2025, these households paid roughly $823 for their drinking water, while those hooked up to public water systems paid just $494 — a roughly 67 percent difference. Water bill inflation in some states was especially egregious. In Maryland, Louisiana, and West Virginia, drinking water costs grew twice as quickly as the states’ median household incomes over the last decade. Corporate water prices have long been disproportionately high. The average bill for households on public systems in 2025 was still less than the $501 those on private systems paid 10 years ago.
